Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-1-prompt-long-0024-reverse-111", "row_sha256": "d5edbd4466f3e2b130681f9e24a1de73a87e7b7323aca66b12286154911ab328", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
hey, could you turn these notes into a clear exhibit brief for the design team at Bellweather Local Museum? it is for the proposed exhibit about work along the Bellweather Canal, and the brief needs to stay within what the notes actually say. the working title is “Night Shift: Work Along Bellweather Canal.” the period is 1938 to 1964. the museum is in the old canal district, but don't say the whole exhibit is about the museum building; it isn't. the local focus is the canal-side warehouses and the people who worked around them. we are not asking for finished wall labels or a finished exhibit plan, just a brief that makes the scope and materials understandable to the team.

background notes: Warehouse 4 was built beside the canal in 1938 and was used for storing dry goods. The notes say it was converted into a cold-storage warehouse in 1951; they don't give a reason for the change. The building closed in 1964. Don't say all the warehouses closed then, only Warehouse 4. The canal carried freight through the district, and workers loaded and unloaded goods at several warehouses. We have no figures for how many people worked there, or how much freight passed through, so don't include numbers for those. The exhibit may describe a working waterfront and the changes to one building, but it shouldn't imply that every worker had the same experience or job.

one source note says the night shift ran from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. at Warehouse 4 in the 1950s. another source note lists common goods as flour, canned fruit, and machine parts. “common” is the word in the note, not an exhaustive inventory, so don't turn the list into everything the warehouse handled. A catalog card from the museum identifies a hand truck, an enamel lunch tin, and a brass time clock as objects associated with the warehouse. The card doesn't say who owned them, and none of the objects is individually connected to a named interviewee. The design team should be able to tell from the brief which details are from the catalog card and which come from the interviews.

interview notes, please keep the quotes exactly as quoted and show the speaker names. Dalia Moreno worked as a packer at Warehouse 4 from 1953 to 1958. she said, “The clock was loud enough to hear from the loading door.” She also recalled that the floor felt cold in winter, but the quote about the clock is the only direct quotation from Dalia in this packet. Don't make up other words for her. Omar Bell drove a delivery truck on the canal road from 1949 to 1962, not as a Warehouse 4 employee. he said, “You could smell the river before you saw the water.” That's his only supplied direct quote too. Don't imply he worked in the warehouse or connect his quote to a particular shift.

there is one more interview, from Ruth Ibarra, whose mother worked at Warehouse 4. Ruth did not work there herself. she said, “My mother kept her lunch tin by the back steps.” We don't have the mother's name, job title, or dates of employment. keep that relationship clear and don't present Ruth as an eyewitness to the workplace. The museum has not identified the lunch tin in the catalog card as Ruth's mother's; in fact the card doesn't identify an owner. So don't connect that object to her family as a fact. It might be worth noting the mismatch between the interview and catalog material for the team, but don't resolve it for them.

please organize the brief so it opens with a short statement of the exhibit's subject and date range, then explains what it should cover and what it should not claim. Include the warehouse history, night-shift schedule, common-goods note, and the three catalog objects. Make the difference between Warehouse 4's closure and the wider canal district clear. Include the three interview excerpts as supplied, with names and the roles or relationships in these notes. The brief should be useful for planning a local-history exhibit, not written as finished visitor-facing copy. We don't need a dramatic story or a conclusion about whether the change to cold storage was good or bad.

maybe use a numbered section for the source material so it is easy to check. It would help to distinguish the background notes, the catalog card, and the interviews, rather than blending them into one account. Keep the distinction between what's stated and what's unknown. In particular, there aren't workforce or freight totals, we don't know why Warehouse 4 changed use, and the objects aren't assigned to any interviewee. The district's other warehouses shouldn't be given dates or outcomes that aren't in these notes.

Send the draft to Leonie, not Ellis. Please make the intended recipient explicit in the prompt for the draft; Ellis is not the recipient. The requested deliverable is one exhibit brief for the design team, with enough source detail to review its scope. It should use the working title as given, retain the stated dates, and include the quotes rather than paraphrasing them. The last part can mention that the team has no supplied information about the mother's identity or employment dates, and that the lunch tin's owner remains unidentified in the catalog. Leave that as a source limitation, not a proposed solution or a finding.", "output": "Create one exhibit brief for the design team at Bellweather Local Museum. Use the working title “Night Shift: Work Along Bellweather Canal.” The exhibit concerns work along the canal, particularly canal-side warehouses and the people who worked around them, during 1938–1964. The museum is in the old canal district, but the exhibit is not about the museum building. Write a planning brief that explains the scope and materials; do not write finished wall labels or a finished exhibit plan.

### Scope and background

Warehouse 4 was built beside the canal in 1938 and used to store dry goods. It was converted into a cold-storage warehouse in 1951, though the notes give no reason for the change. Warehouse 4 closed in 1964. Do not imply that all the district’s warehouses closed then, or assign dates or outcomes to the other warehouses. The canal carried freight through the district, and workers loaded and unloaded goods at several warehouses. The materials provide no workforce totals or freight volumes. Describe the working waterfront and the changes to Warehouse 4 without implying that all workers had the same job or experience.

A source note says that Warehouse 4’s night shift ran from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. in the 1950s. Another lists flour, canned fruit, and machine parts as common goods. Treat this as a list of common goods, not an exhaustive inventory. Do not add other goods or quantities.

### 1. Source materials

**Museum catalog card:** The card identifies a hand truck, an enamel lunch tin, and a brass time clock as objects associated with Warehouse 4. It does not identify their owners, and it does not connect any object to a named interviewee. Distinguish catalog-card information from interview material in the brief.

**Interview excerpts:** Keep each quotation exactly as supplied, identify its speaker, and include the role or relationship stated in the notes.

- Dalia Moreno worked as a packer at Warehouse 4 from 1953 to 1958. She recalled that the floor felt cold in winter. Her supplied direct quotation is: “The clock was loud enough to hear from the loading door.” Do not invent additional words for her.
- Omar Bell drove a delivery truck on the canal road from 1949 to 1962. He was not a Warehouse 4 employee. His supplied direct quotation is: “You could smell the river before you saw the water.” Do not imply that he worked in the warehouse or connect his quote to a particular shift.
- Ruth Ibarra’s mother worked at Warehouse 4; Ruth did not work there herself. Ruth’s supplied direct quotation is: “My mother kept her lunch tin by the back steps.” The notes do not provide the mother’s name, job title, or employment dates. Do not present Ruth as an eyewitness to the workplace.

The interview and catalog materials do not establish that the lunch tin associated with Warehouse 4 belonged to Ruth’s mother. The catalog card leaves its owner unidentified. You may note this difference for the team, but do not resolve it or connect the object to her family as fact.

Explain the exhibit’s coverage and its limits, distinguishing the background notes, catalog card, and interviews rather than blending them into one account. Retain the stated dates and include the supplied quotations rather than paraphrasing them. Keep unknown details unknown: the reason for Warehouse 4’s conversion, the district’s workforce and freight totals, and the objects’ owners are not supplied. Do not add a dramatic story or conclude whether the conversion to cold storage was good or bad.

Send the draft to Leonie, not Ellis. Make the intended recipient explicit. The final part of the brief should state that the materials do not identify Ruth’s mother or give her employment dates, and that the catalog does not identify the lunch tin’s owner. Present these as source limitations, not as a proposed solution or a finding."}]
